USA.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: The US should pursue negotiations with China while maintaining the current tariff structure as leverage. The trade war has already escalated to cover roughly half of bilateral trade ($250 billion in tariffs on Chinese goods), and further escalation risks significant collateral damage to US firms operating in China, US agricultural exporters, and global supply chains. The US should seek a structured deal that addresses IP theft, forced technology transfer, and market access while offering partial tariff relief as an incentive.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: The threat to US interests is moderate (0.25) — the trade war is causing real but contained damage. Soybean prices are down 20%, Midwest farmers are hurting, and US companies operating in China face collateral damage (Brookings). However, the overall US economy impact is described as 'a minor blip' (Brookings), and the US has significant leverage: tariffs cover only half of bilateral trade, and Trump has threatened to tariff the remaining $267 billion (Fox Business). China has retaliated on nearly all US exports to China ($110 billion of $130 billion), showing they are near the end of their tariff ammunition. The action score of -1.0 reflects the need to maintain maximum pressure while pursuing talks — the current tariff structure is the US's primary bargaining chip. China's willingness to 'buy more products and open more markets' (Brookings) suggests a deal is possible. However, the Washington Post reports that negotiations have been complicated by crossed signals and Trump vetoing previous deals, so the US should engage directly at the highest level to avoid further miscommunication. The risk of further escalation is that it would cover 100% of bilateral trade, which would significantly increase costs for US consumers and businesses.
key_factors: $250 billion in US tariffs already in place covering ~50% of bilateral trade
China has retaliated on $110B of $130B in US exports — near exhaustion of tariff options
Soybean prices down 20%, agricultural sector under pressure
US firms operating in China face collateral damage
China willing to negotiate on purchases and market access
Trump has threatened to tariff remaining $267B if China retaliates further
Previous trade deals vetoed by Trump, complicating negotiations

sources_cited.excerpt: The U.S. has announced $250 billion of tariffs on products from China, and China has partially retaliated and will probably come out with more retaliation. For the next several months we will probably be locked into this situation. No high-level negotiations are scheduled.

sources_cited.source_id: www.foxbusiness.com — The U.S.-China Trade War, Explained
sources_cited.excerpt: President Trump has said that if China were to take retaliatory action on these tariffs, which they have, in fact, that he's going to put in place another $267 billion worth of imports. For all intents and purposes, that would put a tariff in place on 100% of U.S.-China trade.

sources_cited.source_id: www.washingtonpost.com — How the U.S. and China misread the signals in the trade war
sources_cited.excerpt: Chinese leaders believed they had a trade agreement last year with Commerce Secretary Wilbur Ross, only to see President Trump veto it. In May, they reached a second deal with Treasury Secretary Steven Mnuchin, but Trump again turned thumbs down — this time via Twitter.

CHN.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: China should signal willingness to engage in substantive negotiations while maintaining current retaliatory tariffs as leverage. We should not escalate further but neither should we make unilateral concessions. The December 1 G20 truce created a 90-day window; we should use it to propose concrete offers on market access and IP protection that address US concerns without sacrificing core industrial policy goals like Made in China 2025.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: The threat to China is significant but not existential at this stage. The US has imposed tariffs on $250 billion of Chinese goods (roughly half of bilateral trade), and Trump has threatened to tariff the remaining $267 billion if China retaliates further (Fox Business, Sept 2018). China has already retaliated on $110 billion of the $130 billion in US imports, covering nearly all bilateral trade. The tariff escalation has hit China's export economy, but the evidence shows China is actively diversifying — lowering tariffs on non-US goods to redirect supply chains away from American products (Fox Business). Soybean prices are down 20% hurting US farmers, and US sectors like autos, agriculture, and Boeing are feeling real pain (Brookings, Dollar). This gives China leverage.

However, the threat is real: China's export-dependent manufacturing hubs face unemployment risk, and the broader uncertainty is dampening investment. The Washington Post reporting (Oct 2018) reveals that previous Chinese offers were rejected by Trump, suggesting the US side is internally divided and unpredictable — making unilateral concessions risky since they may not be reciprocated. The G20 dinner on Dec 1 produced a 90-day truce, which is an opening but not a resolution.

The action_score of -1 (negotiate, at the lower end of the band) reflects that China should engage actively but from a position of firmness, not weakness. We have retaliatory capacity, domestic political support for standing firm, and the US faces its own costs. Conceding now would signal weakness and invite further demands. But refusing to talk would allow the US to justify further escalation. The optimal path is structured negotiation with concrete proposals that address legitimate US concerns (market access, IP) while protecting strategic sectors.
key_factors: US tariffs cover $250B of Chinese exports, roughly half of bilateral trade; Trump threatens to tariff remaining $267B
China has retaliated on nearly all $130B of US imports to China, leaving little room for further tariff retaliation
US domestic sectors (agriculture, autos, Boeing) are experiencing real pain, giving China negotiating leverage
Previous Chinese offers were rejected by Trump administration, suggesting internal US divisions and unpredictability
G20 Dec 1 truce created 90-day negotiation window that should be utilized
China is actively diversifying trade away from US by lowering tariffs on non-US goods
Export-dependent manufacturing regions in China face employment risk from prolonged trade war

The price of soybeans is already down 20 percent... U.S. exports to China are concentrated in agricultural products like soybeans, plus automobiles and Boeing aircraft sales

while they've increased the tariffs on American goods, they've lowered the tariffs on some of the other goods from other places... That's an effort to try to drive their own consumers away from choosing U.S. products and choosing others
